ety.text: PIE word *pénkʷe Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe Proto-Germanic *fimf Proto-West Germanic *fimf Old English fīf Middle English fyf English five From Middle English fyf, fyve, from Old English fīf (“five”), from Proto-West Germanic *fimf (“five”), from Proto-Germanic *fimf (“five”), from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe.

senses.d: A numerical value equal to 5; the number following four and preceding six.
ex: The r-stems had apparently been reduced to the five nuclear kinship terms that still survive in Modern English.

senses.d: Describing a group or set with five elements.

ex: He wrote a five followed by four zeroes.

senses.d: A banknote with a denomination of five units of currency.
ex: Can anyone here change a five?

senses.d: Anything measuring five units, as length.
ex: All the fives are over there in the corner, next to the fours.

senses.d: A person who is five years old.
ex: The fives and sixes will have a snack first, then the older kids.

senses.d: A short rest, especially one of five minutes.
A basketball team, club or lineup.

ety.text: From Middle French cinq, from Old French cinc, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, dissimilation of Classical Latin quīnque (“five”), from Proto-Italic *kʷenkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish cinco, Italian cinque. Doublet of punch.
Inherited from Old Spanish çinco, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, from Latin quīnque. Doublet of ponche and ponzu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cinco~cinquo~cinque, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, from Latin quīnque. Distantly, a doublet of ponche.

phr: and I claim my five pounds
